title: Accuracy vs. Interpretability in Designer-Level Fashion Classification
subtitle: Designer-level fashion classification with interpretability analysis
summary: Studied how model complexity and training strategies impact model performance on deisgner classification and model interpretability.

glance.oneLiner: Designer-level fashion classification that pairs accuracy metrics with interpretability checks to see what the models truly learn.
glance.problem: Runway images make designer labels look easy, but models can win by memorizing scene context (lighting, floor texture, venue layout) instead of garment details. We want to separate real garment understanding from background shortcuts.
glance.approach: Use the iDesigner runway dataset and compare a standard ResNet family with two lightweight FashionNet variants. We test three training setups: original images, background-removed images, and heavy augmentation. We inspect model attention with Grad-CAM and probe embeddings using nearest-neighbor retrieval to see what features cluster.
glance.results: Accuracy is highest on unmasked data, yet attention often lands on the runway rather than the clothing. Masking shifts attention onto garments but reduces accuracy, especially for smaller models. Augmentation recovers some accuracy while only partially reducing background reliance.
takeaways: Background shortcuts inflate accuracy on runway images; interpretability checks are essential.
Masking yields cleaner garment-focused features but needs enough model capacity to avoid large accuracy drops.
Augmentation helps reduce shortcuts, but masking is the stronger push toward garment-centric reasoning.
Feature-space neighbors cluster by garment cues like color and pattern, not just by scene context.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Fashion imagery blends structured cues (garments, textures, silhouettes) with wide variation in pose, lighting, styling, and scene context. That mix makes fine-grained classification challenging and raises questions about what visual cues models truly rely on.

We study how model capacity affects both accuracy and interpretability in designer-level classification. Our guiding questions are: how complex a model is needed for strong accuracy, how complex it must be to learn meaningful and interpretable features, and how those features can be used to analyze fashion itself.

We compare multiple ResNet baselines with a lightweight custom model and probe attention via Grad-CAM and feature-space retrieval. Early high accuracy often reflected background shortcuts; to counter this, we used DeepLab-based segmentation to remove runway context, enabling a cleaner test of garment-centric representations and reframing the later analysis around interpretability under reduced contextual bias.

callout.label: Key finding
callout.text: Unmasked training yields high accuracy but heavy background reliance. Masking improves garment-centric attention but causes large drops for low-capacity models. Aggressive augmentation helps but does not fully remove shortcuts.

sections.title: Dataset
paragraphs: We use the iDesigner FGVC dataset from CVPR 2019: 50,000 high-resolution runway images labeled by designer across major fashion houses. The diversity of designers makes the task visually rich and fine-grained, while the standard crop keeps substantial runway context around the model.

afterFirstFigureParagraphs: We found models often relied on background cues such as runway textures, lighting, and venue architecture rather than garment details. This motivated a background-subtracted variant so performance would reflect garment-level understanding.
We applied a DeepLab person-segmentation model (trained on COCO) to produce binary masks, remove background pixels, and retain only the model and garments for analysis.
afterParagraphs: This segmented dataset provides a cleaner foundation for evaluating the link between model capacity, interpretability, and true visual understanding of fashion features.

sections.title: Model Architectures
paragraphs: We evaluate three families of CNNs: ResNet-18/34/50 baselines and two lightweight custom models, FashionNet-Small and FashionNet-Medium. The custom models are designed to emphasize local textures and silhouettes while remaining more interpretable than large residual networks.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: Our methods cover model design, masking and augmentation pipelines, and a shared training/evaluation protocol. We compare ResNet-18/34/50 baselines (scratch and ImageNet-pretrained) against two custom models: FashionNet-Small (~1M params) and FashionNet-Medium (~5M), built to emphasize localized garment cues while remaining more interpretable than large residual networks.

After midterm analysis showed strong background reliance, we introduced a masking pipeline using DeepLabV3-ResNet-101 (COCO-trained) to isolate the person and remove runway context. We also tested a complementary strategy on unmasked data using heavy augmentation to weaken spurious background correlations.

All models use cross-entropy loss with SGD or Adam, trained for ~40 epochs with step or cosine schedules based on stability. We report top-1 validation accuracy and interpretability via Grad-CAM and nearest-neighbor retrieval in feature space; occlusion tests yielded similar qualitative trends and are omitted.
bullets: Phase I: Baseline training on unmasked images to establish accuracy and shortcut risk.
Phase II: Masked training with background removed to enforce garment-centric learning.
Phase III: Heavy augmentation on unmasked data to reduce background dependence without re-masking.
Augmentations: random crop/resize, strong color jitter, flips + perspective transforms, multi-scale random erasing, and coarse noise masks.

sections.title: Results: Phase I (Unmasked)
paragraphs: On the unmasked dataset, pretrained ResNet-50 achieves the best accuracy, and pretraining consistently boosts all ResNet baselines. When trained from scratch, both FashionNet variants outperform scratch ResNets, suggesting the lightweight models readily exploit stable dataset cues.
afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM reveals those gains are not garment-centric: activations frequently concentrate on runway floor, lighting gradients, and peripheral context rather than the clothing. This indicates strong background–label correlations and motivates masking in Phase II.

sections.title: Results: Phase II (Masked)
paragraphs: Masking removes runway context and forces reliance on garment shape, texture, and silhouette. Accuracy drops sharply across all models; pretrained ResNets remain most robust, while FashionNet-Small and -Medium degrade toward chance, signaling capacity limits under garment-only cues.
afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM shifts toward the garment even when masked-trained models are evaluated on unmasked images, suggesting masking encourages less context-dependent representations.

figures.caption: Figure IV: Grad-CAM result on masked images.

sections.title: Results: Phase III (Heavy Augmentation)
paragraphs: Heavy augmentation on unmasked images recovers much of the performance lost in the masked setting. Pretrained ResNets remain strong; FashionNet-Medium improves more reliably than FashionNet-Small, indicating modest capacity helps benefit from augmentation.
afterTableParagraphs: Grad-CAM shows only partial mitigation: attention moves somewhat toward garments, but runway and scene regions still contribute, implying residual contextual shortcuts.

sections.title: Feature-Space Interpretability
paragraphs: To probe what the model learns beyond accuracy, we run nearest-neighbor retrieval in feature space using FashionNet-Medium trained on the masked dataset. We extract penultimate-layer embeddings, normalize them, and compare examples with cosine similarity to retrieve top neighbors from the training set, showing both ground-truth and predicted designer labels.

Across examples, neighbors often share color palettes, fabric textures, silhouettes, and overall aesthetic structure with the query, even when designer labels differ. Similar layering, drape, or pattern geometry appears repeatedly, suggesting the representation organizes images by visually salient garment attributes rather than coarse scene context. Figure \ref{fig:nn-examples} shows representative matches.

Importantly, these embeddings come from a model trained only on masked images but evaluated on the original unmasked dataset. Even with background restored, neighbor structure remains garment-focused, reinforcing that masking trades off accuracy but yields a more semantically meaningful feature space for fashion analysis.

figures.caption: Figure VI–IX: Feature-space retrieval examples (color similarity; pattern/texture similarity).

sections.title: Takeaways
bullets: Unmasked training delivers high accuracy but relies heavily on background context rather than garments.
Segmentation-based masking shifts attention to garment features (Grad-CAM and neighbor retrieval) but hurts low-capacity models.
Larger and pretrained architectures are more robust when contextual cues are removed.
Masking is effective for fashion-oriented interpretability, but requires sufficient model capacity to balance accuracy.
